New in ML Workshop @ NeurIPS 2026

Retrieval-Guided Fine-Tuning as Noisy Estimation: Risk bounds and Architectural Analysis

Bhargav Lad Affiliation: Department of Mathematics Affiliation: Indian Institute of Technology Delhi Affiliation: New Delhi, India Email: mt6240942@iitd.ac.in    Yifan Hao Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Affiliation: Urbana, IL 61801 Email: yifanh12@illinois.edu
Abstract

Retrieval-Guided Fine-Tuning (RAG-FT) incorporates retrieved data directly into the training objective, but the statistical consequences of noisy retrieval during training remain theoretically undercharacterized. We study this question by modeling RAG-FT as an estimation problem in a multi-task linear regression framework, using an OLS proxy for single-layer linear self-attention to obtain finite-sample risk bounds. Under homoscedastic retrieval noise, we show that retrieval failure decays exponentially with task separation relative to noise, and derive explicit finite-sample conditions under which RAG-FT achieves lower risk than both target-only and full-corpus training. We then introduce a Distance-Proportional Noise (DPN) model, in which retrieval quality degrades with rank, and compare two estimators under the same retrieval process: the OLS proxy and the literal, uniform-weight forward pass of linear self-attention. We prove that the attention estimator’s bias diverges as Θ⁡(n2​q)\Theta(n^{2q}) even under exact retrieval, while OLS risk remains Θ⁡(d/n)\Theta(d/n) for every noise exponent q>0q>0. These results locate the instability not in noisy retrieval itself, but in the fixed, unweighted aggregation of the literal LSA forward pass, which reweighting by reliability empirically removes. We validate the predicted rate separation through direct simulation of the DPN model.

1 Introduction

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds language model predictions in external knowledge by conditioning on retrieved documents at inference time (Lewis et al., 2020). Because model parameters remain fixed at deployment, generalization depends entirely on what fits in the context window at test time, and performance degrades when retrieved passages are topically related but parametrically misaligned with the query (Levy et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024). This has motivated Retrieval-Guided Fine-Tuning (RAG-FT), which incorporates retrieved documents directly into the fine-tuning objective rather than the inference-time context, forcing parametric adaptation to retrieved data (Zhang et al., 2024b; Patil et al., 2024; Asai et al., 2024). Despite its empirical adoption, the statistical mechanics of RAG-FT remain uncharacterized: whether moving retrieval from inference time to training time changes the generalization limits of noisy retrieval is an open question. The closest theoretical treatment (Guo et al., 2025) analyzes inference-time RAG under frozen weights; we ask what changes once the retrieved data instead drives a parameter update.

We study this question in a multi-task linear regression framework where a retriever selects which task’s data to pool with the target dataset for fine-tuning. Motivated by Zhang et al. (2024a), who show that linear self-attention trained on an exchangeable context converges to the ordinary least squares solution, we assume the fine-tuned estimator coincides with this OLS solution on the pooled data (an OLS proxy). This decouples the statistics of retrieval from optimization dynamics and lets us derive exact, finite-sample risk bounds.

Contributions.

We formalize RAG-FT as a stochastic estimation problem in a multi-task linear regression framework, using an OLS proxy for single-layer linear self-attention.

  1. (i)

    We give explicit, finite-sample conditions on task separation and retrieval accuracy under which RAG-FT achieves strictly lower expected risk than both target-only and full-corpus training, compared against each baseline’s true risk rather than a looser bound (Theorem 3).

  2. (ii)

    Under a distance-proportional noise model, we show the OLS proxy’s risk remains Θ⁡(d/n)\Theta(d/n) for every noise exponent q>0q>0, while the literal, uniform-weight linear self-attention forward pass has bias diverging as Θ⁡(n2​q)\Theta(n^{2q}) regardless of retrieval outcome or ambient dimension (Theorems 4, 5).

  3. (iii)

    We validate both rate separations, the dimension-independence of the divergence, and its recovery under a reweighted forward pass, via direct simulation of the generative model (Section 6).

2 Related work

A line of work on in-context learning shows that transformers trained on linear-regression instances implicitly execute ordinary least squares in-context (Garg et al., 2022; Akyürek et al., 2022; Von Oswald et al., 2023), that trained linear self-attention provably converges to this OLS solution but fails under covariate shift (Zhang et al., 2024a), and that this convergence emulates preconditioned gradient descent (Ahn et al., 2023; Mahankali et al., 2024); we adopt this OLS proxy but depart from the i.i.d. setting by modeling the heteroscedastic noise and distributional shift that stochastic retrieval introduces. Separately, retrieval-augmented generation has moved from an inference-time mechanism (Lewis et al., 2020), known to be susceptible to noisy or irrelevant context (Levy et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Yoran et al., 2023), toward methods that push retrieval directly into training: RAFT (Zhang et al., 2024b), Retriever-Aware Training (Patil et al., 2024), Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024), context compression (Xu et al., 2023), and end-to-end retrieval-augmented training (Izacard et al., 2023), none of which give a formal account of how retrieval reshapes the bias-variance tradeoff during parameter updates. The closest theoretical precursor is (Guo et al., 2025), which derives finite-sample generalization bounds for inference-time RAG under distance-proportional noise and establishes a retrieval ceiling n∗=Θ⁡(d1/(2​q))n^{*}=\Theta(d^{1/(2q)}) for a frozen-weight estimator; we study the same distance-proportional noise model once retrieval instead drives a parameter update. Our framework further builds on excess-risk bounds for multi-task and heterogeneous representation learning (Tripuraneni et al., 2021; Maurer et al., 2016; Solnon et al., 2012), on debiasing techniques for noisy or label-corrupted ICL (Liang et al., 2025), and on Bayesian views of in-context algorithm selection (Bai et al., 2023; Ahuja and Lopez-Paz, 2023), which together motivate treating retrieval as a stochastic selection operator with a quantifiable failure rate.

3 Problem setup

Multi-task data model.

We consider a multi-task linear regression framework with K≥2K\geq 2 tasks, indexed by k∈[K]:={1,…,K}k\in[K]:=\{1,\dots,K\}, each associated with a parameter vector θk∈ℝd\theta_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} satisfying ‖θk‖≤B\|\theta_{k}\|\leq B. Let k⋆∈[K]k^{\star}\in[K] denote the (unknown) target task. Data for task kk are generated i.i.d. from the Gaussian linear model

y=x⊤​θk+ε,x∼𝒩⁡(0,Id),ε∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2),x⟂ε.y=x^{\top}\theta_{k}+\varepsilon,\quad x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}),\quad\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}),\quad x\perp\varepsilon.

Task kk contributes a dataset Dk={(xi(k),yi(k))}i=1nD_{k}=\{(x_{i}^{(k)},y_{i}^{(k)})\}_{i=1}^{n}, and the query (target) dataset D′={(xj′,yj′)}j=1mD^{\prime}=\{(x_{j}^{\prime},y_{j}^{\prime})\}_{j=1}^{m} is generated from θk⋆\theta_{k^{\star}}; all datasets {Dk}k=1K\{D_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} and D′D^{\prime} are mutually independent. We quantify task heterogeneity via the minimum and maximum distance from the target task, Δmin:=mink≠k⋆⁡‖θk−θk⋆‖2\Delta_{\min}:=\min_{k\neq k^{\star}}\|\theta_{k}-\theta_{k^{\star}}\|_{2} and Δmax:=maxk≠k⋆⁡‖θk−θk⋆‖2\Delta_{\max}:=\max_{k\neq k^{\star}}\|\theta_{k}-\theta_{k^{\star}}\|_{2}, which respectively set the difficulty of identifying the target task under noise and bound the worst-case bias under retrieval failure.

Retrieval operator.

A retriever selects an index k^∈[K]\hat{k}\in[K] prior to fine-tuning, using only the observed data {Dk}k=1K\{D_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} and D′D^{\prime}; the true parameters {θk}\{\theta_{k}\} and k⋆k^{\star} are never observed by the retriever or the estimator. Here we treat the retriever as a black box, characterized entirely by its failure probability δ:=P⁡(k^≠k⋆)\delta:=P(\hat{k}\neq k^{\star}); equivalently, let R∈{0,1}R\in\{0,1\} be Bernoulli with P⁡(R=1)=1−δP(R=1)=1-\delta, where R=1R=1 denotes correct retrieval, so that the retrieved dataset is DR=Dk⋆D_{R}=D_{k^{\star}} if R=1R=1 and DR=DkD_{R}=D_{k} for some k≠k⋆k\neq k^{\star} if R=0R=0. The results of this section hold for any retriever satisfying this definition; Section 4.1 later fixes a concrete decision rule, based on comparing per-task OLS estimates, and derives an explicit finite-sample bound on δ\delta for it.

RAG-FT estimator and OLS proxy.

Given D′D^{\prime} and DRD_{R}, the pooled dataset is Dpool:=D′∪DRD_{\text{pool}}:=D^{\prime}\cup D_{R}, and the retrieval-guided fine-tuning estimator is the empirical risk minimizer θ^FT:=arg⁡min⁡∑(x,y)∈Dpoolθ⁡(y−x⊤​θ)2\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{FT}}:=\arg\min_{\theta}\sum_{(x,y)\in D_{\text{pool}}}(y-x^{\top}\theta)^{2}. Because θ^FT\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{FT}} is obtained by optimizing a non-convex objective under architectures such as linear self-attention, and because retrieval induces statistical dependence between D′D^{\prime} and DRD_{R} that violates standard i.i.d. assumptions, we decouple the statistics of retrieval from the optimization dynamics via the following structural assumption.

Assumption 1 (OLS Proxy).

The estimator θ^FT\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{FT}} coincides with the exact ordinary least squares solution on the pooled dataset:

θ^FT=(Xpool⊤​Xpool)−1​Xpool⊤​Ypool,\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{FT}}=(X_{\text{pool}}^{\top}X_{\text{pool}})^{-1}X_{\text{pool}}^{\top}Y_{\text{pool}},

where (Xpool,Ypool)(X_{\text{pool}},Y_{\text{pool}}) are the design matrix and response vector formed from DpoolD_{\text{pool}}.

Risk functional.

For a fresh sample (x,y)(x,y) drawn from the target model y=x⊤​θk⋆+εy=x^{\top}\theta_{k^{\star}}+\varepsilon, the prediction risk of an estimator θ^\hat{\theta} is ℛ⁡(θ^):=𝔼(x,y)​[(y−x⊤​θ^)2]\mathcal{R}(\hat{\theta}):=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)}[(y-x^{\top}\hat{\theta})^{2}]. Our objective is to characterize 𝔼⁡[ℛ⁡(θ^FT)]\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{R}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{FT}})], jointly over the data-generating process and the retrieval randomness. Since θ^FT\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{FT}} depends on RR, the law of total expectation gives

𝔼⁡[ℛ⁡(θ^FT)]=(1−δ)​𝔼​[ℛ⁡(θ^FT)∣R=1]+δ​𝔼​[ℛ⁡(θ^FT)∣R=0],\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{R}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{FT}})]=(1-\delta)\,\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{R}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{FT}})\mid R=1]+\delta\,\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{R}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{FT}})\mid R=0],

separating the variance reduction from pooling homogeneous target-task data (R=1R=1) from the bias incurred by pooling heterogeneous data under retrieval failure (R=0R=0).

4 Theoretical analysis: under homoscedastic retrieval noise

To rigorously evaluate the generalization of Retrieval-Guided Fine-Tuning (RAG-FT), we first isolate the statistical penalty of task mismatch from distance-dependent noise by assuming a uniform homoscedastic retrieval regime. This controlled setting quantifies how selective retrieval navigates the fundamental bias-variance tradeoff in multi-task environments.

We first bound the retrieval failure probability (Section 4.1), formalize the expected prediction risk (Section 4.2), and define the exact conditions where RAG-FT achieves a statistical advantage over standard baselines (Section 4.3).

4.1 Finite-sample risk decomposition (failure probability)

Assumption 2 (Uniform Homoscedastic Noise).

For all candidate tasks k∈[K]k\in[K], we assume the task datasets DkD_{k} are corrupted by independent, identically distributed Gaussian noise ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}).

By fixing the variance scale across all datasets, this assumption strictly isolates the generalization penalty to the geometric bias induced by task mismatch, decoupling it from heteroscedastic effects (addressed later in Section 5).

Lemma 1 (Distribution of OLS Estimation Noise).

Under Gaussian design xi∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)x_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) and homogeneous noise ϵi∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2)\epsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}), the OLS estimator for any task kk (including the target query qq) satisfies θ^k−θk|Xk∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​(Xk⊤​Xk)−1)\hat{\theta}_{k}-\theta_{k}\mid X_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\sigma^{2}(X_{k}^{\top}X_{k})^{-1}\right).

Lemma 2 (Signal-Fluctuation Decomposition).

For any incorrect candidate task k≠k∗k\neq k^{\ast}, let TkT_{k} denote the empirical distance gap evaluated by the nearest-estimator retrieval rule. This decision statistic decomposes exactly into a deterministic geometric signal and two stochastic error terms:

Tk:=‖θ^k−θ^q‖22−‖θ^k∗−θ^q‖22⏟Empirical distance gap=‖θk−θk∗‖22⏟Geometric signal+Lk⏟Linear fluctuation+Qk⏟Quadratic fluctuationT_{k}:=\underbrace{\left\|\hat{\theta}_{k}-\hat{\theta}_{q}\right\|_{2}^{2}-\left\|\hat{\theta}_{k^{*}}-\hat{\theta}_{q}\right\|_{2}^{2}}_{\text{Empirical distance gap}}=\underbrace{\left\|\theta_{k}-\theta_{k^{*}}\right\|_{2}^{2}}_{\text{Geometric signal}}+\underbrace{L_{k}}_{\text{Linear fluctuation}}+\underbrace{Q_{k}}_{\text{Quadratic fluctuation}}

where LkL_{k} and QkQ_{k} are the estimation noise fluctuations bounded in auxiliary Lemmas 3 and 4 (Appendix B).

Bounding the sub-Gaussian tail of LkL_{k} (Lemma 3) and the sub-exponential tail of QkQ_{k} (Lemma 4) around the geometric signal ‖θk−θk∗‖22\|\theta_{k}-\theta_{k^{\ast}}\|_{2}^{2} yields the finite-sample failure probability.

Theorem 1 (Finite-Sample Bound on Retrieval Failure).

Let the minimum task separation satisfy Δmin2≥C1​σ2​d/n\Delta_{\min}^{2}\geq C_{1}\sigma^{2}d/n for a constant C1>0C_{1}>0. The retrieval failure probability δ=ℙ⁡(k^≠k∗)\delta=\mathbb{P}(\hat{k}\neq k^{*}) satisfies

δ≤3​(K−1)​exp⁡(−C​min⁡{Δmin4ν¯ 2,Δmin2α¯})+3​K​exp⁡(−c′​d),\delta\leq 3(K-1)\exp\!\left(-C\min\!\left\{\frac{\Delta_{\min}^{4}}{\bar{\nu}^{\,2}},\frac{\Delta_{\min}^{2}}{\bar{\alpha}}\right\}\right)+3K\exp(-c^{\prime}d),

where C,c′>0C,c^{\prime}>0 are universal constants, ν¯ 2=O⁡(σ2​Δmax2/n+d​σ4/n2)\bar{\nu}^{\,2}=O\!\left(\sigma^{2}\Delta_{\max}^{2}/n+d\sigma^{4}/n^{2}\right), and α¯=O⁡(σ​Δmax/n+σ2/n)\bar{\alpha}=O\!\left(\sigma\Delta_{\max}/\sqrt{n}+\sigma^{2}/n\right).

Assuming target sample size m=Ω⁡(n)m=\Omega(n), query-side estimation noise is absorbed into ν¯2\bar{\nu}^{2} and α¯\bar{\alpha}. Theorem 1 demonstrates that failure probability decays exponentially once the geometric task separation Δmin2\Delta_{\min}^{2} overcomes the finite-sample estimation noise scale, leaving only an irreducible O⁡(K​exp⁡(−c′​d))O(K\exp(-c^{\prime}d)) probability of ill-conditioned designs. Notably, scaling the candidate corpus (K→∞K\to\infty) forces failure unless separation grows as log⁡K\log K. Ultimately, the effective bottleneck is governed by the signal-to-noise ratio Δmin2​n/σ2\Delta_{\min}^{2}n/\sigma^{2} in the proportional regime.

4.2 Risk bounds: success vs. failure risk decomposition

With the retrieval failure probability δ\delta bounded, we establish the expected prediction risk of the retrieval-guided estimator θ^FT\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{FT}}. As introduced in Section 3, conditioning on the retrieval outcome R∈{0,1}R\in\{0,1\} isolates the competing statistical forces of the RAG-FT mechanism.

When retrieval succeeds (R=1R=1), the estimator benefits from pure variance reduction.

Proposition 1 (Risk under Successful Retrieval).

Conditioned on the success event R=1R=1, the estimator θ^FT\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{FT}} fits m+nm+n homogeneous samples drawn strictly from the target task {θk∗}\{\theta_{k^{*}}\}. The estimator is unbiased, and under the good design event ℰgood\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}} with m+n≥(1+η0)​dm+n\geq(1+\eta_{0})d for some η0>0\eta_{0}>0, its conditional risk satisfies the two-sided bound

σ2+σ2​dm+n−d−1≤𝔼⁡[ℛ⁡(θ^FT)∣R=1]≤σ2+C​σ2​dm+n,\sigma^{2}+\sigma^{2}\,\frac{d}{m+n-d-1}\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\mathcal{R}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{FT}})\mid R=1\Bigr]\;\leq\;\sigma^{2}+C\sigma^{2}\,\frac{d}{m+n},

where the lower bound is the exact inverse-Wishart trace identity 𝔼⁡[Tr⁡((X⊤​X)−1)]=d/(m+n−d−1)\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Tr}((X^{\top}X)^{-1})]=d/(m+n-d-1), valid unconditionally for m+n>d+1m+n>d+1, and C>0C>0 is a universal constant governing the upper bound under ℰgood\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}}.

When retrieval fails (R=0R=0), the estimator fits a single linear model to a heterogeneous dataset, inducing a high geometric bias.

Proposition 2 (Risk under Retrieval Failure).

Conditioned on the failure event R=0R=0, in the high-dimensional proportional regime where d∝(m+n)d\propto(m+n) and m+n>dm+n>d, the conditional risk satisfies

𝔼⁡[ℛ⁡(θ^FT)∣R=0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathcal{R}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{FT}})\mid R=0\right] ≥σ2+σ2​dm+n−d−1+(nm+n)2​Δmin2,\displaystyle\geq\sigma^{2}+\sigma^{2}\frac{d}{m+n-d-1}+\left(\frac{n}{m+n}\right)^{2}\Delta_{\min}^{2},
𝔼⁡[ℛ⁡(θ^FT)∣R=0]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathcal{R}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{FT}})\mid R=0\right] ≤σ2+C​σ2​dm+n+C​(nm+n)2​(1−dm+n)−2​Δmax2,\displaystyle\leq\sigma^{2}+C\sigma^{2}\frac{d}{m+n}+C\left(\frac{n}{m+n}\right)^{2}\left(1-\frac{d}{m+n}\right)^{-2}\Delta_{\max}^{2},

where the lower bound holds unconditionally (for m+n>d+1m+n>d+1), the upper bound holds under the good design event ℰgood\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}} with m+n≥(1+η0)​dm+n\geq(1+\eta_{0})d for some η0>0\eta_{0}>0, and C>0C>0 is a universal constant.

Both propositions isolate the same two statistical forces. Successful retrieval pools m+nm+n homogeneous samples, achieving the exact inverse-Wishart variance floor d/(m+n−d−1)d/(m+n-d-1). Retrieval failure pools a heterogeneous dataset, inducing a geometric bias scaled by the mixture proportion n/(m+n)n/(m+n) and amplified by high-dimensional spectral inflation (1−d/(m+n))−2(1-d/(m+n))^{-2}.

Combining these exact conditional bounds with the unconditional failure probability δ\delta yields the core statistical guarantee of RAG-FT under uniform noise.

Theorem 2 (Total Expected Risk Bound for RAG-FT).

Under the uniform homoscedastic noise assumption, let the ambient dimension scale proportionally as d∝(m+n)d\propto(m+n) with m+n>dm+n>d. The expected prediction risk of the retrieval-guided fine-tuning estimator θ^FT\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{FT}}, evaluated on a fresh sample from the target task, satisfies

𝔼⁡[ℛ⁡(θ^FT)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[\mathcal{R}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{FT}})\big] ≥σ2+σ2​dm+n−d−1+δ​(nm+n)2​Δmin2,\displaystyle\geq\sigma^{2}+\sigma^{2}\frac{d}{m+n-d-1}+\,\delta\left(\frac{n}{m+n}\right)^{2}\Delta_{\min}^{2},
𝔼⁡[ℛ⁡(θ^FT)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[\mathcal{R}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{FT}})\big] ≤σ2+C1​σ2​dm+n+C2​δ​(nm+n)2​(1−dm+n)−2​Δmax2,\displaystyle\leq\sigma^{2}+C_{1}\sigma^{2}\frac{d}{m+n}+C_{2}\,\delta\left(\frac{n}{m+n}\right)^{2}\left(1-\frac{d}{m+n}\right)^{-2}\Delta_{\max}^{2},

where C1,C2>0C_{1},C_{2}>0 are universal constants, δ\delta is the retrieval failure probability bounded in Theorem 1, and the lower bound is unconditional, with the exact variance floor following from the inverse-Wishart identities underlying Propositions 1 and 2 (valid for m+n>d+1).

This bound illustrates how RAG-FT interpolates between target-only fine-tuning and full-corpus aggregation. The bias penalty enters only upon retrieval failure, strictly gated by δ\delta. Because δ\delta decays exponentially with sufficient task separation, RAG-FT achieves a favorable bias-variance trade-off precisely in this well-separated regime.

4.3 Strict dominance over training baselines

To contextualize the RAG-FT guarantees, we compare against two standard paradigms: fine-tuning on the target dataset alone, and fine-tuning on the full heterogeneous corpus. These represent the extremes of the bias-variance tradeoff. Target-only training provides an unbiased estimator but suffers high variance 𝒪⁡(d/m)\mathcal{O}(d/m). Conversely, full-corpus aggregation minimizes variance to 𝒪⁡(d/Nfull)\mathcal{O}(d/N_{\mathrm{full}}) but introduces an irreducible bias. Specifically, unless tasks are adversarially anti-correlated, pooling KK tasks forces a population bias proportional to the minimum task separation Δmin2\Delta_{\min}^{2}. The formal risk bounds for these baselines (Propositions 3 and 4, alongside the necessary bounded anti-correlation assumption) are deferred to Appendix B.5.

We establish the exact conditions where RAG-FT strictly dominates both baselines simultaneously by comparing the upper bound of Theorem 2 against the lower bounds of the standard estimators.

Writing Nfull:=K​n+mN_{\mathrm{full}}:=Kn+m, Λ:=(m+n−d)2C2​n2​Δmax2\Lambda:=\dfrac{(m+n-d)^{2}}{C_{2}\,n^{2}\Delta_{\max}^{2}}, and g⁡(N):=1N−d−1−C1m+ng(N):=\dfrac{1}{N-d-1}-\dfrac{C_{1}}{m+n} for N>d+1N>d+1, define the critical thresholds

δtarget:=Λ​σ2​d​g​(m),δfull:=Λ⁡(σ2​d​g​(Nfull)+(nNfull)2​(K−1)​[1−(K−2)​ρ]​Δmin2).\delta_{\mathrm{target}}:=\Lambda\,\sigma^{2}d\,g(m),\qquad\delta_{\mathrm{full}}:=\Lambda\left(\sigma^{2}d\,g(N_{\mathrm{full}})+\left(\frac{n}{N_{\mathrm{full}}}\right)^{2}(K-1)\big[1-(K-2)\rho\big]\Delta_{\min}^{2}\right).
Theorem 3 (Strict Dominance of RAG-FT).

Let the expected risks of the standard baselines be bounded as in Appendix B.5, the full-corpus bound under Assumption 3. In the high-dimensional proportional regime d∝(m+n)d\propto(m+n) with m+n>dm+n>d, retrieval-guided fine-tuning strictly outperforms both target-only and full-corpus fine-tuning if

δ<min⁡{δtarget,δfull}.\delta<\min\{\delta_{\mathrm{target}},\delta_{\mathrm{full}}\}.

Both thresholds must be positive for the claim to be non-vacuous; Remark 3 gives the precise conditions.

Theorem 3 demonstrates that RAG-FT achieves a favorable bias-variance trade-off whenever task separation and sample size are jointly sufficient to drive the retrieval failure probability below these critical thresholds (which is guaranteed by Theorem 1).

The homoscedastic model is, however, a structural idealization. In practice, the noise variance scales with retrieval rank, and the uniform-weight constraint of linear self-attention cannot accommodate this. Section 5 examines the consequences.

5 Theoretical analysis: under heteroscedastic retrieval noise

Section 4 shows that RAG-FT navigates the bias-variance tradeoff well under homoscedastic noise: the failure probability δ\delta decays exponentially in Δmin2\Delta_{\min}^{2}, and the induced bias is attenuated accordingly. That result rests on Assumption 2, which assigns every candidate dataset the same noise variance σ2\sigma^{2} regardless of its distance from the query, an idealization real corpora violate, since retrieval quality varies systematically with rank. This section replaces that idealization with a distance-proportional noise model and compares how two estimators of the same retrieval process respond to it.

5.1 The Distance-Proportional Noise (DPN) model

Let xq∈ℝdx_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the query covariate, xq∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)x_{q}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}). Retrieved samples are indexed by rank i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\dots,n\}, with i=1i=1 the nearest neighbor under the retrieval metric. Each retrieved covariate is modeled as

xrag(i)=xq+ri,ri∼𝒩⁡(0,δi2​Id),x_{\mathrm{rag}}^{(i)}=x_{q}+r_{i},\qquad r_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\delta_{i}^{2}I_{d}),

where rir_{i} is an independent Gaussian offset encoding the geometric displacement from the query at rank ii, mutually independent across ii and independent of both xqx_{q} and the label noise. Conditional on xqx_{q}, xrag(i)∼𝒩⁡(xq,δi2​Id)x_{\mathrm{rag}}^{(i)}\sim\mathcal{N}(x_{q},\delta_{i}^{2}I_{d}); since δi2\delta_{i}^{2} varies with rank, the retrieved covariates are neither i.i.d. across ii nor marginally standard Gaussian.

The label model for a retrieved sample pooled from task kk is

yi=(xrag(i))⊤​θk+ϵi,𝔼⁡[ϵi∣xrag(i)]=0,Var⁡(ϵi∣xrag(i))=σi2,y_{i}=(x_{\mathrm{rag}}^{(i)})^{\top}\theta_{k}+\epsilon_{i},\qquad\mathbb{E}[\epsilon_{i}\mid x_{\mathrm{rag}}^{(i)}]=0,\qquad\mathrm{Var}(\epsilon_{i}\mid x_{\mathrm{rag}}^{(i)})=\sigma_{i}^{2},

where θk\theta_{k} is the parameter of whichever task was retrieved, coinciding with θk⋆\theta_{k^{\star}} under successful retrieval and differing from it otherwise, as in Section 4.

Power-law retrieval geometry.

Semantic relevance degrades with retrieval rank. We model this with a shared power-law scaling of the covariate offset and the label noise:

δi2=γ​iq,σi2=γ​σ2​iq,q>0,\delta_{i}^{2}=\gamma i^{q},\qquad\sigma_{i}^{2}=\gamma\sigma^{2}i^{q},\qquad q>0,

where γ>0\gamma>0 sets the scale and qq governs the rate of noise growth; coupling the two exponents ensures noisier labels are also, geometrically farther from the query. This yields independent noise variables εi∼𝒩⁡(0,γ​σ2​iq)\varepsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\gamma\sigma^{2}i^{q}), with covariance matrix

Ω:=Var⁡(ε∣X)=diag⁡(γ​σ2⋅1q,γ​σ2⋅2q,…,γ​σ2⋅nq).\Omega:=\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon\mid X)=\mathrm{diag}\!\left(\gamma\sigma^{2}\cdot 1^{q},\;\gamma\sigma^{2}\cdot 2^{q},\;\ldots,\;\gamma\sigma^{2}\cdot n^{q}\right).

Ω\Omega is diagonal but non-uniform, violating the homoscedasticity required for OLS to be the optimal linear estimator.

5.2 OLS risk under Distance-Proportional Noise

We now turn to the OLS proxy under the DPN model of Section 5.1. To isolate the effect of retrieval volume from the proportional dimensional scaling used for the OLS baselines of Section 4, we hold the ambient dimension dd, the target sample size mm, and the noise exponent q>0q>0 fixed, and let only the retrieval volume nn grow.

Theorem 4 (OLS Risk under DPN).

Under the DPN model, with dd, mm, and q>0q>0 fixed and n→∞n\to\infty, the prediction-risk variance of the OLS proxy,

VOLS​(n):=Tr⁡[(X⊤​X)−1​(X⊤​Ω​X)​(X⊤​X)−1],V_{\mathrm{OLS}}(n):=\mathrm{Tr}\!\left[(X^{\top}X)^{-1}(X^{\top}\Omega X)(X^{\top}X)^{-1}\right],

the Huber–White sandwich covariance trace of Theorem A.4, where X∈ℝ(m+n)×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{(m+n)\times d} is the pooled design and Ω∈ℝ(m+n)×(m+n)\Omega\in\mathbb{R}^{(m+n)\times(m+n)} is the pooled noise covariance (diagonal, with target entries σ2\sigma^{2} and retrieved entries σrag,i2=γ​σ2​iq\sigma_{\mathrm{rag},i}^{2}=\gamma\sigma^{2}i^{q}), satisfies

𝔼⁡[VOLS​(n)]=d​σ2​(q+1)22​q+1⋅1n​(1+o⁡(1))=Θ⁡(dn).\mathbb{E}[V_{\mathrm{OLS}}(n)]=\frac{d\,\sigma^{2}(q+1)^{2}}{2q+1}\cdot\frac{1}{n}\,(1+o(1))=\Theta\!\left(\frac{d}{n}\right).

for every fixed noise exponent q>0q>0, and no divergence occurs at any qq.

Proof sketch. The pooled design matrix decomposes as a mean term μ​Id+n​xq​xq⊤\mu I_{d}+n\,x_{q}x_{q}^{\top} (μ=m+sn=Θ⁡(nq+1)\mu=m+s_{n}=\Theta(n^{q+1})) plus a fluctuation of operator norm O⁡(d​nq+1/2)O(\sqrt{d}\,n^{q+1/2}), negligible relative to the mean for every q>0q>0. The mean term is scalar-plus-rank-one and inverts in closed form via Sherman–Morrison; the same decomposition applied to the noise-weighted design X⊤​Ω​XX^{\top}\Omega X yields a matching closed form. Their product has a diagonal trace in the shared eigenbasis that simplifies to d​σ2​(q+1)2/(2​q+1)⋅n−1d\sigma^{2}(q+1)^{2}/(2q+1)\cdot n^{-1} at leading order, with remaining approximation error o⁡(1/n)o(1/n) uniformly in qq.

This absence of divergence mirrors the homoscedastic case of Section 4: OLS’s inverse-covariance correction adapts to whatever noise structure is present, so increasing heteroscedasticity changes the constant in d/nd/n but not the rate. This is the baseline against which Section 5.3 evaluates the literal LSA forward pass.

5.3 LSA risk under Distance-Proportional Noise

Assumption 1 is not invoked in this section: retrieval rank in the DPN model is a fixed index, with covariates at each rank drawn independently of any data-dependent statistic, so no adaptive-selection step stands between the estimator and the data. This lets us study the untrained LSA forward pass directly, alongside the OLS proxy, as two separate, explicitly named estimators of the same DPN process. The following theorem shows the literal estimator behaves very differently from the OLS proxy of Theorem 4.

The literal LSA forward pass produces the prediction y^q=1n​∑i=1n(xq⊤​xrag(i))​yi\hat{y}_{q}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{q}^{\top}x_{\mathrm{rag}}^{(i)})\,y_{i}, a uniform average over the retrieved context with no mechanism to weight ranks by their reliability. Unlike the OLS proxy, this estimator has no matrix inversion step to correct for the noise structure of the pooled data.

Theorem 5 (LSA Risk under DPN).

Under the DPN model, with d,md,m, and q>0q>0 fixed, n→∞n\to\infty, and the retrieved task signal bounded away from zero (‖θk‖≥b0\|\theta_{k}\|\geq b_{0} for some fixed constant b0>0b_{0}>0), the literal LSA forward-pass estimator has prediction risk

ℛLSA​(n)=σ2+𝔼⁡[Bias​(xq)2]+𝔼⁡[Var⁡(y^q∣xq)],\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{LSA}}(n)=\sigma^{2}+\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Bias}(x_{q})^{2}]+\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Var}(\hat{y}_{q}\mid x_{q})],

where both terms admit finite-nn expressions (Appendix C.2, exact for the bias, leading-order for the variance) and satisfy, as n→∞n\to\infty for every fixed q>0q>0,

𝔼⁡[Bias​(xq)2]=Θ⁡(n2​q),𝔼⁡[Var⁡(y^q∣xq)]=Θ⁡(d⋅n2​q−1).\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Bias}(x_{q})^{2}]=\Theta(n^{2q}),\qquad\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Var}(\hat{y}_{q}\mid x_{q})]=\Theta(d\cdot n^{2q-1}).

The bias term dominates the variance term for every fixed q>0q>0 (their ratio is Θ⁡(n/d)→∞\Theta(n/d)\to\infty) and diverges regardless of whether the retrieved task matches the target task, so

ℛLSA​(n)=σ2+Θ⁡(n2​q)+Θ⁡(d⋅n2​q−1)→∞as ​n→∞, for every ​q>0.\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{LSA}}(n)=\sigma^{2}+\Theta(n^{2q})+\Theta(d\cdot n^{2q-1})\to\infty\qquad\text{as }n\to\infty,\text{ for every }q>0.

Proof sketch. Conditioning on xqx_{q} and writing xq=ρ​ωx_{q}=\sqrt{\rho}\,\omega with ω\omega uniform on the unit sphere, the bias 𝔼⁡[y^q∣xq]−xq⊤​θk⋆\mathbb{E}[\hat{y}_{q}\mid x_{q}]-x_{q}^{\top}\theta_{k^{\star}} reduces to a quadratic form in ρ\rho; taking expectation over ρ∼χ2​(d)\rho\sim\chi^{2}(d) gives an exact closed-form second moment whose leading term is governed by (sn/n)2​‖θk‖2(s_{n}/n)^{2}\|\theta_{k}\|^{2}, with sn/n=Θ⁡(nq)s_{n}/n=\Theta(n^{q}) and no dependence on dd at leading order. The variance Var⁡(y^q∣xq)\mathrm{Var}(\hat{y}_{q}\mid x_{q}) combines two independent sources computed via the same conditioning argument, fluctuation of the retrieved offset rir_{i} and label noise ϵi\epsilon_{i}, giving Θ⁡(d⋅n2​q−1)\Theta(d\cdot n^{2q-1}). Since their ratio is Θ⁡(n/d)→∞\Theta(n/d)\to\infty, the bias term governs the total risk for every q>0q>0.

5.4 Architectural separation under DPN

Theorems 4 and 5 describe the same retrieval process through two estimators that respond to it very differently. The OLS proxy’s inverse-covariance correction absorbs whatever heteroscedasticity DPN introduces, so its risk stays Θ⁡(d/n)\Theta(d/n) for every q>0q>0: the constant in front of d/nd/n grows with qq, but the rate does not. The literal LSA forward pass has no such correction; its prediction is a uniform, unweighted average over retrieved context, and under DPN this fixed averaging leaves the bias uncalibrated, diverging as Θ⁡(n2​q)\Theta(n^{2q}) for every q>0q>0 regardless of retrieval outcome. Because this divergence carries no leading-order dependence on dd, it admits no dimension-dependent ceiling of the kind that bounds risk in the frozen-weight setting of (Guo et al., 2025): increasing dd does not restore stability. Within this estimator’s fixed parameterization the gap cannot be closed by choice of attention weights, since uniform averaging is a property of the forward pass we analyze, not a learned quantity; the failure therefore lies in the absence of a reweighting mechanism, not in retrieval or the noise model itself. Figure 2 in the appendix confirms both properties directly.

6 Empirical validation

The homoscedastic results of Section 4 rest on exact finite-sample identities, so we target the asymptotic separation asserted by Theorems 4 and 5. Every Monte Carlo point simulates the generative model of Section 5.1 and evaluates each estimator from its defining formula, never from the closed-form risk expressions plotted as theory curves, so agreement between markers and curves tests the derivation rather than restating it.

Panel (a) sweeps retrieval volume nn at d=20d=20, m=50m=50 for q∈{0.5,1,2}q\in\{0.5,1,2\}. OLS follows the predicted Θ⁡(d/n)\Theta(d/n) decay at every exponent, while LSA turns upward at Θ⁡(n2​q)\Theta(n^{2q}), diverging earlier as qq grows. Panel (b) fixes q=1q=1 and varies the retrieved task: exact retrieval (θk=θk⋆)(\theta_{k}=\theta_{k^{\star}}) diverges at the same rate as two mismatched tasks, the signature of a bias governed by the aggregation rule rather than by retrieval error. Appendix D reports two further predictions of Theorem 5: the rate is unchanged across d∈{5,20,50,100}d\in\{5,20,50,100\}, matching a bias term with no leading-order dd dependence, and reweighting the same forward pass by reliability restores stability exactly where uniform averaging fails (Figure 2).

7 Conclusion

We analyzed Retrieval-Guided Fine-Tuning as a stochastic estimation problem in a multi-task linear regression framework. Under homoscedastic noise, the retrieval failure probability decays exponentially in Δmin2​n/σ2\Delta_{\min}^{2}n/\sigma^{2}, and RAG-FT’s risk bound falls strictly below the lower bounds for target-only and full-corpus training once this failure probability is small enough (Theorems 1–3). Under Distance-Proportional Noise, we separated two estimators of the same retrieval process: the OLS proxy’s risk remains Θ⁡(d/n)\Theta(d/n) for every noise exponent q>0q>0, while the literal LSA forward pass’s bias diverges as Θ⁡(n2​q)\Theta(n^{2q}), dominating its variance and growing regardless of retrieval outcome or ambient dimension (Theorems 4–5). We trace this divergence to the forward pass’s fixed, unweighted aggregation rather than to retrieval noise itself, and confirm both rate separations by direct simulation (Section 6).

8 Limitations

Our analysis rests on several simplifying choices. The OLS proxy for the fine-tuned estimator is an assumption, not something we derive from training dynamics, so our risk bounds hold only to the extent that this proxy is accurate. The LSA divergence in Section 5 is proven for the fixed, untrained forward pass; whether a trained attention layer can learn to reweight retrieved context and close this gap remains an open question. Sections 4 and 5 also use two different asymptotic regimes: one scales dimension with sample size, the other fixes dimension and grows retrieval volume, and we do not unify them. More broadly, the model itself is idealized: it assumes Gaussian covariates, a linear ground-truth relationship, a fixed set of candidate tasks with a single retrieval step, and a specific noise model for retrieval quality, none of which we test against real retrieval corpora or trained non-linear models. Finally, our finite-sample bounds involve unspecified constants and are thus not numerically tight, and the full-corpus baseline requires a bounded task anti-correlation condition.

Appendix A Technical preliminaries

This section collects the standard results from high-dimensional probability and random matrix theory that are invoked in the proofs of the main theorems. Statements are given in the forms used in this paper; we refer the reader to the cited sources for generality and proof.

Several proofs condition on the event that the relevant design matrix is well-conditioned. For a design matrix X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} with i.i.d. rows drawn from 𝒩⁡(0,Id)\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), and a fixed constant C0>0C_{0}>0, define the good design event

ℰgood:={∥(X⊤X)−1∥op≤C0/n}.\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}}\;:=\;\bigl\{\|(X^{\top}X)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq C_{0}/n\bigr\}.

The design matrix and sample size nn instantiating this event vary by context: in Theorem 1, XX ranges over the per-task design matrices XkX_{k} with nn the per-task sample size; in Propositions 1–4, XX is the relevant pooled design matrix, with nn replaced by m+nm+n, mm, or NN as appropriate.

Theorem A.1 (Gaussian Tail Bound).

Let Z∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}). For any t>0t>0,

ℙ⁡(Z≤−t)≤exp⁡(−t22​σ2).\mathbb{P}(Z\leq-t)\;\leq\;\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{t^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\Bigr).

This bound is applied in Step 4 of the proof of Theorem 1 to control the probability that the linear fluctuation term LkL_{k} falls below a threshold determined by the task separation Δmin\Delta_{\min}. See Vershynin (2018) for a standard reference.

Theorem A.2 (Hanson–Wright Inequality (Rudelson and Vershynin, 2013)).

Let Z=(Z1,…,Zp)⊤∈ℝpZ=(Z_{1},\ldots,Z_{p})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} be a random vector with independent, mean-zero, sub-Gaussian components satisfying ‖Zi‖ψ2≤K\|Z_{i}\|_{\psi_{2}}\leq K. Let A∈ℝp×pA\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p} be a fixed symmetric matrix. Then there exists an absolute constant c>0c>0 such that for all t>0t>0,

ℙ⁡(|Z⊤​A​Z−𝔼⁡[Z⊤​A​Z]|≥t)≤ 2​exp⁡(−c​min⁡{t2K4​‖A‖F2,tK2​‖A‖op}).\mathbb{P}\bigl(|Z^{\top}AZ-\mathbb{E}[Z^{\top}AZ]|\geq t\bigr)\;\leq\;2\exp\!\left(-c\min\!\left\{\frac{t^{2}}{K^{4}\|A\|_{F}^{2}},\,\frac{t}{K^{2}\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}}\right\}\right).

In the proof of Lemma 4, the quadratic fluctuation term Qk=Z⊤​M​ZQ_{k}=Z^{\top}MZ is expressed as a quadratic form in the concatenated OLS error vector Z∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma), and Theorem A.2 is applied with A=Σ1/2​M​Σ1/2A=\Sigma^{1/2}M\Sigma^{1/2} to obtain its sub-exponential tail bound. The Frobenius and operator norms of this symmetrized matrix contribute the quadratic-fluctuation term to ν2\nu^{2} and α\alpha in Theorem 1.

Theorem A.3 (Marchenko–Pastur Law).

Let X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} have i.i.d. rows drawn from 𝒩⁡(0,Id)\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), and let κ=d/n∈(0,1)\kappa=d/n\in(0,1) be fixed as n→∞n\to\infty. The empirical spectral distribution of 1n​X⊤​X\frac{1}{n}X^{\top}X converges weakly to the Marchenko–Pastur distribution with ratio κ\kappa, supported on [(1−κ)2,(1+κ)2][(1-\sqrt{\kappa})^{2},(1+\sqrt{\kappa})^{2}]. In the proportional regime d∝nd\propto n, the following non-asymptotic moment estimate holds: under the good design event ℰgood\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}}, there exists a constant C>0C>0 such that

𝔼⁡[Tr⁡((X⊤​X)−1)|ℰgood]≤C​dn,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{Tr}((X^{\top}X)^{-1})\;\big|\;\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}}\bigr]\;\leq\;\frac{Cd}{n},

and the spectral norm of the inverse satisfies

𝔼⁡[‖(X⊤​X)−1‖op|ℰgood]≤Cn​(1−dn)−2.\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|(X^{\top}X)^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;\big|\;\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}}\bigr]\;\leq\;\frac{C}{n}\!\left(1-\frac{d}{n}\right)^{-2}.

The trace bound is used in the proof of Proposition 1 to bound the effective variance 𝔼x​[x⊤​(X⊤​X)−1​x]\mathbb{E}_{x}[x^{\top}(X^{\top}X)^{-1}x] under the pooled design matrix. The spectral norm bound appears in the proof of Proposition 2 as the spectral inflation factor (1−d/(m+n))−2(1-d/(m+n))^{-2} amplifying the geometric bias under retrieval failure. Both bounds follow from inverse Wishart moment calculations; see Bai and Silverstein (2009) for the rigorous random matrix treatment and Vershynin (2018) for the non-asymptotic formulation.

Theorem A.4 (Huber–White Covariance Estimator (White, 1980)).

Let θ^=(X⊤​X)−1​X⊤​Y\hat{\theta}=(X^{\top}X)^{-1}X^{\top}Y be the OLS estimator under the heteroscedastic model Y=X​θ∗+εY=X\theta^{*}+\varepsilon with Var⁡(εi∣xi)=σi2\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_{i}\mid x_{i})=\sigma_{i}^{2}. The conditional covariance of θ^\hat{\theta} given XX is

Var⁡(θ^∣X)=(X⊤​X)−1​(∑i=1nσi2​xi​xi⊤)​(X⊤​X)−1.\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}\mid X)\;=\;(X^{\top}X)^{-1}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}^{2}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)\!(X^{\top}X)^{-1}.

Taking expectation over XX with 𝔼⁡[xi​xi⊤]=Id\mathbb{E}[x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}]=I_{d}, and whenever the noise variances are uniformly bounded by σ2\sigma^{2},

𝔼⁡[Tr⁡(Var⁡(θ^∣X))]≤C​σ2​dn.\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Tr}(\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}\mid X))]\leq C\sigma^{2}\frac{d}{n}.

The covariance formula defines VOLS​(n)V_{\mathrm{OLS}}(n) in Theorem 4. Under the DPN model of Section 5.1, where σi2\sigma_{i}^{2} grows with rank and is not uniformly bounded, the trace bound above does not apply directly; the DPN-specific trace bound is instead derived directly in Appendix C.1 via the Sherman–Morrison decomposition, without appeal to this corollary.

Theorem A.5 (Matrix Bernstein Inequality (Vershynin, 2018)).

Let S1,…,Sn∈ℝd×dS_{1},\ldots,S_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} be independent, symmetric, mean-zero random matrices with maxi⁡‖Si‖ψ1≤K\max_{i}\|S_{i}\|_{\psi_{1}}\leq K. Let v:=‖∑i=1n𝔼⁡[Si2]‖opv:=\bigl\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}[S_{i}^{2}]\bigr\|_{\mathrm{op}} denote the matrix variance proxy. Then there exists an absolute constant c>0c>0 such that, with probability at least 1−d−c1-d^{-c},

‖∑i=1nSi‖op=O⁡(v+K).\Bigl\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}S_{i}\Bigr\|_{\mathrm{op}}\;=\;O\bigl(\sqrt{v}+K\bigr).

This inequality is applied in the proofs of Theorem 4 and Theorem 5 to bound the operator norm of the fluctuation terms arising from the rank-dependent covariance structure of the DPN model, where each SiS_{i} is a centered outer product ri​ri⊤−δi2​Idr_{i}r_{i}^{\top}-\delta_{i}^{2}I_{d} (or its noise-weighted analogue), and the variance proxy vv is computed via the Gaussian fourth-moment identity 𝔼⁡[‖z‖2​z​z⊤]=(d+2)​Id\mathbb{E}[\|z\|^{2}zz^{\top}]=(d+2)I_{d} for z∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}).

Theorem A.6 (Sherman–Morrison Identity).

Let A∈ℝd×dA\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} be invertible and u,v∈ℝdu,v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. If 1+v⊤​A−1​u≠01+v^{\top}A^{-1}u\neq 0, then A+u​v⊤A+uv^{\top} is invertible and

(A+u​v⊤)−1=A−1−A−1​u​v⊤​A−11+v⊤​A−1​u.(A+uv^{\top})^{-1}\;=\;A^{-1}-\frac{A^{-1}uv^{\top}A^{-1}}{1+v^{\top}A^{-1}u}.

This identity is applied in the proofs of Theorem 4 and Theorem 5 to invert the conditional-mean design matrix Σ¯=μ​Id+n​xq​xq⊤\bar{\Sigma}=\mu I_{d}+n\,x_{q}x_{q}^{\top} in closed form.

Theorem A.7 (Exact Inverse Wishart Trace Identity).

Let X∈ℝN×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} have i.i.d. rows drawn from 𝒩⁡(0,Id)\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), with N>d+1N>d+1. Then X⊤​XX^{\top}X follows a Wishart distribution 𝒲d​(N,Id)\mathcal{W}_{d}(N,I_{d}), and

𝔼⁡[Tr⁡((X⊤​X)−1)]=dN−d−1.\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{Tr}((X^{\top}X)^{-1})\bigr]\;=\;\frac{d}{N-d-1}.

This is the exact first moment of the inverse Wishart distribution and holds without any high-probability conditioning, unlike the Marchenko–Pastur trace bound of Theorem A.3, which is a conditional upper bound valid under the good design event. The exact identity is used to establish the variance lower bound in Propositions 1 and 2, and their analogues for the target-only and full-corpus baselines in Section 4.3.

Lemma A.1 (Concentration of Empirical Covariance).

Under Gaussian design X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} with i.i.d. rows drawn from 𝒩⁡(0,Id)\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), in the proportional regime n≥c0​dn\geq c_{0}d for a fixed constant c0>0c_{0}>0, there exists c′>0c^{\prime}>0 such that

ℙ⁡(ℰgoodc)≤ 3​exp⁡(−c′​d).\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}}^{c})\;\leq\;3\exp(-c^{\prime}d).

This is a standard consequence of non-asymptotic random matrix concentration; see Vershynin (2018), Chapter 4. Applying this bound to each of the KK per-task design matrices individually and taking a union bound gives ℙ⁡(ℰgoodc)≤3​K​exp⁡(−c′​d)\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}}^{c})\leq 3K\exp(-c^{\prime}d) for the intersection event used in Theorem 1, representing the irreducible high-dimensional bottleneck that persists even with infinite task data.

ℙ⁡(ℰ|𝒳)≤ 3​(K−1)​exp⁡(−C​min⁡{Δmin4ν2,Δmin2α}).\mathbb{P}\!\left(\mathcal{E}\;\middle|\;\mathcal{X}\right)\;\leq\;3(K-1)\exp\!\left(-C\min\!\left\{\frac{\Delta_{\min}^{4}}{\nu^{2}},\;\frac{\Delta_{\min}^{2}}{\alpha}\right\}\right).

Step 8: Removing the conditioning via the good design event. The bounds in Steps 4–6 rely on the conditional variance parameters ν2\nu^{2} and α\alpha, which are well-defined only when the empirical covariance matrices (Xk⊤​Xk)−1(X_{k}^{\top}X_{k})^{-1} are well-conditioned. Define the good design event

ℰgood:={∥(Xk⊤Xk)−1∥op≤C0n for all k∈[K]}\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}}\;:=\;\left\{\bigl\lVert(X_{k}^{\top}X_{k})^{-1}\bigr\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\frac{C_{0}}{n}\;\text{ for all }k\in[K]\right\}

for a fixed constant C0>0C_{0}>0.

By Lemma A.1, each individual event ℰk:={∥(Xk⊤Xk)−1∥op≤C0/n}\mathcal{E}_{k}:=\{\|(X_{k}^{\top}X_{k})^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq C_{0}/n\} satisfies ℙ⁡(ℰkc)≤3​exp⁡(−c′​d)\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{k}^{c})\leq 3\exp(-c^{\prime}d). Since ℰgood=⋂k=1Kℰk\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}}=\bigcap_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{E}_{k}, a union bound over the KK tasks gives

ℙ⁡(ℰgoodc)=ℙ⁡(⋃k=1Kℰkc)≤∑k=1Kℙ⁡(ℰkc)≤3​K​exp⁡(−c′​d).\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}}^{c})=\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{E}_{k}^{c}\Bigr)\leq\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{k}^{c})\leq 3K\exp(-c^{\prime}d).

The law of total probability then gives

δ=ℙ⁡(ℰ)\displaystyle\delta\;=\;\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}) ≤ℙ⁡(ℰ|ℰgood)​ℙ​(ℰgood)+ℙ⁡(ℰgoodc)\displaystyle\;\leq\;\mathbb{P}\!\left(\mathcal{E}\;\middle|\;\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}}\right)\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}})\;+\;\mathbb{P}\!\left(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}}^{c}\right)
≤ℙ⁡(ℰ|ℰgood)+ℙ⁡(ℰgoodc)\displaystyle\;\leq\;\mathbb{P}\!\left(\mathcal{E}\;\middle|\;\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}}\right)\;+\;\mathbb{P}\!\left(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}}^{c}\right)
≤ 3​(K−1)​exp⁡(−C​min⁡{Δmin4ν2,Δmin2α})+ 3​K​exp⁡(−c′​d),\displaystyle\;\leq\;3(K-1)\exp\!\left(-C\min\!\left\{\frac{\Delta_{\min}^{4}}{\nu^{2}},\;\frac{\Delta_{\min}^{2}}{\alpha}\right\}\right)\;+\;3K\exp(-c^{\prime}d),

where the last inequality substitutes the conditional bound from Step 7 and the good design concentration estimate. This is the claimed bound, completing the proof. ∎

Remark 1.

The expected bias penalty in Theorem 2 is gated by δ\delta and therefore decays exponentially in the signal-to-noise ratio Δmin2​n/σ2\Delta_{\min}^{2}n/\sigma^{2} once the task separation exceeds the estimation noise floor. In the well-separated regime Δmin2≫σ2​d/n\Delta_{\min}^{2}\gg\sigma^{2}\sqrt{d/n}, the bias term is negligible and the bound reduces to σ2+𝒪⁡(d/(m+n))\sigma^{2}+\mathcal{O}(d/(m+n)), recovering the same rate as Proposition 1. Conversely, in the degenerate regime δ→1\delta\to 1, arising when the task corpus is dense and Δmin\Delta_{\min} is small, the bias penalty dominates and the bound degrades to the full failure-mode risk of Proposition 2. The factor (1−d/(m+n))−2\left(1-d/(m+n)\right)^{-2} quantifies the spectral amplification of the geometric bias by near-singular empirical covariances in the proportional high-dimensional regime; it diverges as d/(m+n)→1d/(m+n)\to 1, confirming that the estimator requires m+n≫dm+n\gg d to remain stable.

B.5 Baseline risk bounds (target-only and full-corpus)

In this section, we formally state and prove the risk bounds for the two standard fine-tuning baselines discussed in Section 4.3: target-only fine-tuning and full-corpus fine-tuning.

Proposition 3 (Risk of Target-Only Fine-Tuning).

Let θ^target\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{target}} denote the OLS estimator trained exclusively on the query dataset 𝒟′\mathcal{D}^{\prime} of mm i.i.d. samples from the target task θk∗\theta_{k^{*}}, with m>d+1m>d+1. The expected prediction risk satisfies

σ2+σ2​dm−d−1≤𝔼⁡[ℛ⁡(θ^target)]≤σ2+C1​σ2​dm,\sigma^{2}+\sigma^{2}\frac{d}{m-d-1}\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathcal{R}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{target}})\bigr]\;\leq\;\sigma^{2}+C_{1}\sigma^{2}\frac{d}{m},

where the lower bound is the exact inverse-Wishart identity and the upper bound holds under the good design event ℰgood\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}} with m≥(1+η0)​dm\geq(1+\eta_{0})d for some η0>0\eta_{0}>0.

Proof of Proposition 3. The target-only estimator θ^target\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{target}} is OLS on mm homogeneous samples from θk∗\theta_{k^{*}}, which is exactly the setting of Proposition 1 with n=0n=0. The two-sided bound follows immediately, provided m>d+1m>d+1. ∎

The full-corpus bias bound below requires ruling out exact cancellation among opposing task deviations.

Assumption 3 (Bounded Task Anti-Correlation).

For K≥3K\geq 3, there exists ρ∈[0, 1/(K−2))\rho\in[0,\,1/(K-2)) such that the task deviations δk:=θk−θk∗\delta_{k}:=\theta_{k}-\theta_{k^{*}} satisfy

⟨δi,δj⟩≥−ρΔmin2,i≠j,i,j∈[K]∖{k∗}.\langle\delta_{i},\delta_{j}\rangle\geq-\rho\,\Delta_{\min}^{2},\qquad i\neq j,\quad i,j\in[K]\setminus\{k^{*}\}.

No such assumption is required when K=2K=2.

Remark 2.

Assumption 3 rules out only the degenerate case in which task deviations are strongly and systematically opposed. It is automatically satisfied whenever the {δk}\{\delta_{k}\} are not adversarially anti-correlated (for instance, whenever all pairwise inner products are non-negative, the boundary case ρ=0\rho=0 applies). Without some assumption of this form, the full-corpus population bias can vanish by exact cancellation: e.g. for K=2K=2 with δ1=−δ2\delta_{1}=-\delta_{2}, the population target θ¯full\bar{\theta}_{\mathrm{full}} coincides with θk∗\theta_{k^{*}} even though ‖δ1‖=‖δ2‖=Δmin>0\|\delta_{1}\|=\|\delta_{2}\|=\Delta_{\min}>0. Assumption 3 is the weakest condition of this kind that restores a non-trivial lower bound for K≥3K\geq 3, requiring ρ<1/(K−2)\rho<1/(K-2); for K=2K=2 there are no cross terms and no anti-correlation assumption is needed.

Proposition 4 (Risk of Full-Corpus Fine-Tuning).

Let θ^full\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{full}} denote the OLS estimator trained on the pooled dataset 𝒟′∪⋃k=1K𝒟k\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\cup\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{D}_{k} of Nfull=m+K​nN_{\mathrm{full}}=m+Kn samples. Define the population minimizer of the full-corpus mixture loss as

θ¯full:=m​θk∗+n​∑k=1Kθkm+K​n,\bar{\theta}_{\mathrm{full}}:=\frac{m\,\theta_{k^{*}}+n\sum_{k=1}^{K}\theta_{k}}{m+Kn},

so that θ^full\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{full}} is unbiased for θ¯full\bar{\theta}_{\mathrm{full}} in expectation over the random design (not conditionally, for a fixed design realization). Under Assumption 3 and in the high-dimensional proportional regime d∝Nfulld\propto N_{\mathrm{full}} with Nfull>dN_{\mathrm{full}}>d, the expected prediction risk satisfies

σ2+σ2​dNfull−d−1+(nNfull)2​(K−1)​[1−(K−2)​ρ]​Δmin2\displaystyle\sigma^{2}+\sigma^{2}\frac{d}{N_{\mathrm{full}}-d-1}+\left(\frac{n}{N_{\mathrm{full}}}\right)^{\!2}(K-1)\bigl[1-(K-2)\rho\bigr]\,\Delta_{\min}^{2}
≤𝔼⁡[ℛ⁡(θ^full)]\displaystyle\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathcal{R}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{full}})\bigr]
𝔼⁡[ℛ⁡(θ^full)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathcal{R}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{full}})\bigr] ≤σ2+C1​σ2​dNfull\displaystyle\;\leq\;\sigma^{2}+C_{1}\sigma^{2}\frac{d}{N_{\mathrm{full}}}
+C2​(K​nNfull)2​(1−dNfull)−2​Δmax2,\displaystyle\quad+C_{2}\left(\frac{Kn}{N_{\mathrm{full}}}\right)^{\!2}\left(1-\frac{d}{N_{\mathrm{full}}}\right)^{-2}\Delta_{\max}^{2},

where the lower bound holds unconditionally (for Nfull>d+1N_{\mathrm{full}}>d+1), the upper bound holds under ℰgood\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}} with Nfull≥(1+η0)​dN_{\mathrm{full}}\geq(1+\eta_{0})d for some η0>0\eta_{0}>0, and C2>0C_{2}>0 is a universal constant.

Variance term. Conditional on the design, the randomness from the label noise gives the usual σ2​(Xfull⊤​Xfull)−1\sigma^{2}(X_{\mathrm{full}}^{\top}X_{\mathrm{full}})^{-1} covariance around the empirical conditional mean. The additional mismatch bias is handled separately through the population mixture offset plus the design fluctuation term Δ⁡(Xfull)\Delta(X_{\mathrm{full}}), mirroring the structure in Proposition 2. Thus, the variance from the label noise alone is exactly Var⁡(θ^full∣Xfull)=σ2​(Xfull⊤​Xfull)−1\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{full}}\mid X_{\mathrm{full}})=\sigma^{2}(X_{\mathrm{full}}^{\top}X_{\mathrm{full}})^{-1}. By Theorem A.7 applied to the NN-row Gaussian design matrix,

𝔼⁡[Tr​(Xfull⊤​Xfull)−1]=dN−d−1,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathrm{Tr}(X_{\mathrm{full}}^{\top}X_{\mathrm{full}})^{-1}\bigr]=\frac{d}{N-d-1},

Under ℰgood\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}} with N≥(1+η0)​dN\geq(1+\eta_{0})d, the standard inverse-Wishart upper bound yields 𝔼⁡[Tr​(Xfull⊤​Xfull)−1∣ℰgood]≤C​d/N\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Tr}(X_{\mathrm{full}}^{\top}X_{\mathrm{full}})^{-1}\mid\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}}]\leq Cd/N.

Bias term: upper bound. By the triangle inequality ‖∑k=1Kδk‖≤K​Δmax\bigl\|\sum_{k=1}^{K}\delta_{k}\bigr\|\leq K\Delta_{\max}, so

‖θ¯full−θk∗‖2≤(K​nm+K​n)2​Δmax2.\bigl\|\bar{\theta}_{\mathrm{full}}-\theta_{k^{*}}\bigr\|^{2}\leq\left(\frac{Kn}{m+Kn}\right)^{\!2}\Delta_{\max}^{2}.

In the proportional regime the Marchenko–Pastur spectral norm bound (Theorem A.3) gives 𝔼⁡[‖(Xfull⊤​Xfull)−1‖op∣ℰgood]≤C​(m+K​n)−1​(1−d/N)−2\mathbb{E}[\|(X_{\mathrm{full}}^{\top}X_{\mathrm{full}})^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\mid\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}}]\leq C(m+Kn)^{-1}(1-d/N)^{-2}, amplifying the bias by (1−d/N)−2(1-d/N)^{-2} and establishing the upper bound.

Bias term: lower bound. Expanding the squared norm of the sum exactly via the polarization identity,

‖∑k=1Kδk‖2=∑k=1K‖δk‖2+∑i≠j⟨δi,δj⟩.\Bigl\|\sum_{k=1}^{K}\delta_{k}\Bigr\|^{2}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\|\delta_{k}\|^{2}+\sum_{i\neq j}\langle\delta_{i},\delta_{j}\rangle.

Since δk∗=0\delta_{k^{*}}=0, the first sum is really a sum over k≠k∗k\neq k^{*}, and since ‖δk‖≥Δmin\|\delta_{k}\|\geq\Delta_{\min} for all k≠k∗k\neq k^{*}, it satisfies ∑k≠k∗‖δk‖2≥(K−1)​Δmin2\sum_{k\neq k^{\ast}}\|\delta_{k}\|^{2}\geq(K-1)\Delta_{\min}^{2}. Likewise, any cross term involving k∗k^{*} vanishes identically, so only the (K−1)​(K−2)(K-1)(K-2) cross terms with both indices in [K]∖{k∗}[K]\setminus\{k^{*}\} can contribute. By Assumption 3, each such term satisfies ⟨δi,δj⟩≥−ρ​Δmin2\langle\delta_{i},\delta_{j}\rangle\geq-\rho\,\Delta_{\min}^{2}, so

∑i≠j⟨δi,δj⟩≥−ρ​Δmin2​(K−1)​(K−2).\sum_{i\neq j}\langle\delta_{i},\delta_{j}\rangle\;\geq\;-\rho\,\Delta_{\min}^{2}\,(K-1)(K-2).

Combining,

‖∑k=1Kδk‖2≥(K−1)​Δmin2−ρ⁡(K−1)​(K−2)​Δmin2=(K−1)​[1−ρ⁡(K−2)]​Δmin2,\Bigl\|\sum_{k=1}^{K}\delta_{k}\Bigr\|^{2}\;\geq\;(K-1)\Delta_{\min}^{2}-\rho\,(K-1)(K-2)\Delta_{\min}^{2}\;=\;(K-1)\bigl[1-\rho(K-2)\bigr]\Delta_{\min}^{2},

which is strictly positive since ρ<1/(K−2)\rho<1/(K-2) for K≥3K\geq 3 (for K=2K=2 there is no cross term, and the bound reduces exactly to Δmin2\Delta_{\min}^{2}). Therefore the population squared bias satisfies

‖θ¯full−θk∗‖2≥(nm+K​n)2​(K−1)​[1−ρ⁡(K−2)]​Δmin2.\bigl\|\bar{\theta}_{\mathrm{full}}-\theta_{k^{*}}\bigr\|^{2}\;\geq\;\left(\frac{n}{m+Kn}\right)^{\!2}(K-1)\bigl[1-\rho(K-2)\bigr]\Delta_{\min}^{2}.

Since θ¯full−θk∗\bar{\theta}_{\mathrm{full}}-\theta_{k^{*}} is a fixed vector depending only on the deterministic task parameters {θk}\{\theta_{k}\}, and x∼N⁡(0,Id)x\sim N(0,I_{d}) is independent of XfullX_{\mathrm{full}}, the identity 𝔼x​[(x⊤​(θ¯full−θk∗))2]=‖θ¯full−θk∗‖2\mathbb{E}_{x}[(x^{\top}(\bar{\theta}_{\mathrm{full}}-\theta_{k^{*}}))^{2}]=\|\bar{\theta}_{\mathrm{full}}-\theta_{k^{*}}\|^{2} holds exactly, with no conditioning on ℰgood\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{good}}. Combining variance and bias terms establishes the upper bound; combining the variance floor with the bias lower bound establishes the stated lower bound, up to a further non-negative contribution 𝔼Xfull​[‖Δ⁡(Xfull)‖2]\mathbb{E}_{X_{\mathrm{full}}}[\|\Delta(X_{\mathrm{full}})\|^{2}] from the fluctuation term introduced above, whose exact value again requires matrix-variate second moments beyond the elementary identities used here but whose scale, O⁡(Δmax2​m​K​n/N3)O(\Delta_{\max}^{2}\,mKn/N^{3}), is dominated by the retained bias term in the regime d∝Nd\propto N considered throughout, so omitting it costs nothing qualitative.

Both thresholds require m>d+1m>d+1 (respectively Nfull>d+1N_{\mathrm{full}}>d+1) for the exact inverse-Wishart denominators to be finite and positive, consistent with the preconditions of Propositions 3 and 4. Appendix D Additional empirical validation

This section collects settings and estimator definitions omitted from Section 6 for space.

The divergence of the literal LSA forward pass under distance-proportional noise carries no leading-order dependence on ambient dimension, and is specific to unweighted aggregation rather than to retrieval noise itself. Figure 2 confirms both properties directly.

Methodology.

All Monte Carlo points are obtained by directly simulating the generative model of Section 5.1 and fitting or evaluating each estimator from its literal defining formula (least-squares for OLS, the explicit forward-pass average for LSA and its variants); no Monte Carlo point is computed by numerically evaluating the closed-form risk expressions plotted as theory curves. Each point in Figure 1 and 2(a) averages held-out prediction risk over at least 300 independent seeds, with fresh test queries drawn per seed; Figure 2(b) averages over 300 seeds per retrieval volume nn. Error bars are standard errors across seeds, clipped below at 0.1×0.1\times the mean so that the lower whisker stays positive on the log axis.

Interpretation.

The plotted curves are the finite-nn risk expressions derived in Appendix C.1–C.2, namely the semi-analytic 𝔼​[VOLS​(n)]\mathbb{E}[V_{\mathrm{OLS}}(n)] of Theorem 4 and the exact bias plus leading-order variance of Theorem 5, not the asymptotic rates Θ⁡(d/n)\Theta(d/n) and Θ⁡(n2​q)\Theta(n^{2q}) those expressions reduce to. This matters for interpretation: the theorems are statements about n→∞n\to\infty, so plotting the rates alone would leave the small-nn region untested, whereas the finite-nn expressions are falsifiable at every nn on the grid. The LSA curve is therefore non-monotone at small nn, where the c0c^{0} and c1c^{1} terms of the exact bias still compete with c2c^{2}; the Θ⁡(n2​q)\Theta(n^{2q}) slope emerges only once c=sn/n−1c=s_{n}/n-1 grows large.

Reweighted LSA estimators.

Figure 2(b) evaluates two variants of the forward pass that replace uniform averaging with a reliability-weighted average,

y^q=∑i=1nwi​(xq⊤​xrag(i))​yi∑i=1nwi⋅zi,\hat{y}_{q}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\,(x_{q}^{\top}x_{\mathrm{rag}}^{(i)})\,y_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\cdot z_{i}},

differing only in the weights wiw_{i} and normalizer ziz_{i}:

  • •

    Oracle inverse-variance: wi=1/σrag,i2w_{i}=1/\sigma_{\mathrm{rag},i}^{2} with zi=1z_{i}=1, i.e., the estimator is given the true DPN noise variance at each rank and normalizes by ∑iwi\sum_{i}w_{i}.

  • •

    Self-normalized: wi=1w_{i}=1 with zi=(xq⊤​xrag(i))2z_{i}=(x_{q}^{\top}x_{\mathrm{rag}}^{(i)})^{2}, i.e., the estimator normalizes by the total similarity mass ∑i(xq⊤​xrag(i))2\sum_{i}(x_{q}^{\top}x_{\mathrm{rag}}^{(i)})^{2} rather than by nn, using no information beyond what the uniform forward pass already computes.

Parameter settings.

The table provided below lists the fixed parameters underlying each figure; nn is swept over a log-spaced grid in each case, and θk∗\theta_{k^{*}} is a fixed unit vector throughout.
